name: Plastic bottle
action: Empty and rinse the bottle, crush it if possible, and place it in the recyclable (dry) waste collection.
reuse_idea: Use it as a planter, a storage container or a bird feeder.
eco_tip: Carry a refillable bottle to cut down on single-use plastic.
explanation: Clean plastic bottles are commonly accepted for recycling. Rinsing keeps leftovers from contaminating other recyclables.

name: Plastic bag / polythene
action: Shake out any dirt, keep it dry, and give it with other dry plastic to the recyclable collection. Thin, dirty bags may not be accepted locally.
reuse_idea: Reuse it for carrying items or as a liner for a dry-waste bin.
eco_tip: Switch to a cloth bag and keep it near your door so you remember it.
explanation: Plastic film is recyclable in many places but is light and easily contaminated, so keeping it clean and dry helps.

name: Plastic container / tub
action: Remove food residue, rinse, let it dry, and place it in the recyclable collection.
reuse_idea: Use it to store small items, leftovers or craft supplies.
eco_tip: Reuse containers several times before recycling them.
explanation: Rigid plastic containers are usually recyclable once they are clean.

name: Snack / chips packet
action: Put it in the general (reject) waste bin. Some areas have special collection for multilayer packaging, so check locally.
reuse_idea: Clean wrappers can be used in craft projects, such as woven mats or bags.
eco_tip: Buy larger packs or loose items to reduce small wrappers.
explanation: Packets made of several bonded layers (plastic and foil) are hard to separate, so they are rarely recycled.

name: Newspaper / paper
action: Keep it dry and clean, stack it, and place it in the recyclable (dry) waste collection or give it to a scrap collector.
reuse_idea: Use it for wrapping, packing, craft projects or as drawer liners.
eco_tip: Print on both sides and go digital where you can.
explanation: Clean, dry paper is one of the most commonly recycled materials.

name: Cardboard box
action: Remove tape and packing material, flatten the box, keep it dry, and place it in the recyclable collection.
reuse_idea: Reuse it for storage, shipping, a kids' play house or a seedling tray.
eco_tip: Reuse boxes before recycling them.
explanation: Cardboard is made of paper fibres that can be recycled, as long as it is not soaked with oil or food.

name: Greasy pizza box
action: Tear off any clean, dry top part for recycling. Put the greasy, food-stained part in the general waste, or in wet waste if your area composts paper.
reuse_idea: Use clean parts as a base for crafts or fire-starting only if local rules allow it.
eco_tip: Ask for less packaging, or carry your own container when you can.
explanation: Oil soaks into paper fibres and spoils recycling batches, so the stained part should not go with clean paper.

name: Used tissue paper
action: Put used tissues in the general waste bin. Lightly food-soiled napkins can go with wet waste if your area composts them.
reuse_idea: Use washable cloth napkins and handkerchiefs instead.
eco_tip: Cloth napkins cut down on single-use paper.
explanation: Tissue paper has short fibres and is usually soiled, so it is not recycled.

name: Glass bottle / jar
action: Empty and rinse it, remove the lid, and place it in the recyclable collection or give it to a scrap collector.
reuse_idea: Reuse jars for storing spices, grains or homemade items, or as a candle holder.
eco_tip: Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
explanation: Glass is highly recyclable. Rinsing prevents leftovers from contaminating the batch.

name: Broken glass
action: Wrap the pieces in thick newspaper or cardboard, label it as broken glass, and hand it over with general or reject waste. Never put loose shards in a bin bag.
reuse_idea: Whole, unbroken glass can be reused. Broken pieces should not be reused.
eco_tip: Handle with gloves and sweep carefully so no small pieces are left behind.
explanation: Sharp glass can injure waste collectors, so it needs safe wrapping and clear labelling.

name: Metal can / tin
action: Empty and rinse the can, and place it in the recyclable collection or give it to a scrap collector.
reuse_idea: Use it as a pen holder, a plant pot or a candle holder.
eco_tip: Recycling metal saves much more energy than making it from raw ore.
explanation: Metals can be melted and reused many times, so cans are valuable to recyclers.

name: Aerosol / spray can
action: Do not puncture or burn it. If it is empty, check local rules for metal recycling. If it still has contents, hand it to a hazardous-waste collection point.
reuse_idea: Not recommended for reuse.
eco_tip: Use pump sprays or solid products instead of aerosols.
explanation: Pressurised cans can explode and may hold flammable or harmful contents.

name: Food scraps / leftovers
action: Put it in the wet (green) bin or a home compost bin. Avoid mixing it with plastic.
reuse_idea: Compost it at home, or share edible leftovers with animals only if it is safe to do so.
eco_tip: Plan meals and store food well to reduce what gets thrown away.
explanation: Food is organic and breaks down naturally, so composting turns it into useful soil nutrients instead of landfill waste.

name: Fruit / vegetable peels
action: Add them to the wet-waste bin or a compost pit or bin.
reuse_idea: Make a bio-enzyme cleaner from citrus peels, or use peels as compost for plants.
eco_tip: Keep a small compost bin on your balcony or in your kitchen.
explanation: Peels are plant material that decomposes quickly and enriches compost.

name: Tea leaves / coffee grounds
action: Put used tea leaves and coffee grounds in the wet bin or compost. Remove staples and plastic parts from tea bags first.
reuse_idea: Use cooled tea leaves or coffee grounds as plant fertiliser in small amounts.
eco_tip: Choose loose-leaf tea or plastic-free tea bags.
explanation: These are plant-based and break down easily in compost.

name: Eggshells
action: Crush them and add to compost or the wet-waste bin.
reuse_idea: Crushed shells add calcium to compost and garden soil.
eco_tip: Rinse and dry shells before crushing to avoid smell.
explanation: Eggshells are natural material that slowly breaks down and supports plant growth.

name: Leaves / garden waste
action: Compost them in a pit or bin, or place them in the wet or garden-waste collection. Do not burn them.
reuse_idea: Use dry leaves as mulch around plants or in a compost layer.
eco_tip: Burning leaves pollutes the air, and composting is cleaner and useful.
explanation: Plant matter breaks down naturally and returns nutrients to the soil.

name: Used cooking oil
action: Let it cool, pour it into a sealed container, and give it to a used-cooking-oil collection programme if available. Do not pour it down the sink or drain.
reuse_idea: Some collectors turn used oil into biodiesel, and small amounts can make homemade soap with proper guidance.
eco_tip: Wipe greasy pans with paper before washing to keep oil out of drains.
explanation: Oil blocks pipes and pollutes water, so it should be collected rather than washed away.

name: Used battery
action: Do not put it in the household bin. Take it to a battery or e-waste collection point or a shop that accepts used batteries.
reuse_idea: Use rechargeable batteries to cut the number of cells you throw away.
eco_tip: Tape the terminals of lithium batteries before drop-off to prevent fires.
explanation: Batteries contain metals and chemicals that can leak into soil and water, and damaged lithium batteries can catch fire.

name: Old mobile phone / electronics
action: Wipe personal data, then hand it to an authorised e-waste collector or a take-back programme. Do not put it in the household bin.
reuse_idea: Donate or sell working devices, or repurpose an old phone as a music player or alarm clock.
eco_tip: Repairing and reusing electronics saves more resources than recycling them.
explanation: Electronics contain metals that can be recovered but also harmful materials, so they need specialised handling.

name: Charger / cables / earphones
action: Give it to an authorised e-waste collection point instead of the household bin.
reuse_idea: Keep working chargers as spares, or donate them. Old cables can organise other cords.
eco_tip: Buy durable accessories and repair frayed cables where it is safe to do so.
explanation: Cables and chargers have copper and plastic parts that can be recovered through e-waste recycling.

name: Bulb / CFL / tube light
action: Handle gently so it does not break, and take it to an e-waste or lighting-waste collection point. Do not put it in the household bin.
reuse_idea: Not suitable for reuse once it is broken or fused.
eco_tip: Switch to LED bulbs, which last longer and use less energy.
explanation: CFLs and tube lights may contain a small amount of mercury, so they need safe collection.

name: Expired medicine
action: Do not flush it or throw it in the open. Return it to a pharmacy or health centre with a take-back option, or ask a doctor or pharmacist how to dispose of it safely.
reuse_idea: Do not reuse expired medicine. Recycle the empty, clean packaging if local rules allow it.
eco_tip: Buy only the quantity you need and check expiry dates.
explanation: Medicines can harm people, animals and water if disposed of carelessly.

name: Syringe / sharps
action: Place it in a hard, puncture-proof container and take it to a clinic, hospital or authorised biomedical-waste collector. Never put sharps in a household bin.
reuse_idea: Never reuse.
eco_tip: Ask your healthcare provider about safe sharps disposal.
explanation: Needles and sharps can injure people and spread infection, so they must go to trained handlers.

name: Paint / chemicals
action: Keep it in the original, tightly closed container and take it to a hazardous-waste collection point. Do not pour it down drains or onto soil.
reuse_idea: Give leftover paint to someone who can use it, such as a school or community project.
eco_tip: Buy only the amount of paint you need.
explanation: Paints and chemicals can poison soil and water and can be dangerous to handle.

name: Thermocol / styrofoam
action: Put it in the general (reject) waste unless a local facility specifically accepts foam. Keep it clean and dry.
reuse_idea: Reuse it to pack fragile items or as drainage at the bottom of plant pots.
eco_tip: Ask sellers for paper-based packaging.
explanation: Foam is light and bulky and is rarely recycled, so reusing it before disposal is the best option.

name: Old clothes / textiles
action: Wash and donate wearable items. Give worn-out fabric to a textile-recycling drive or scrap collector.
reuse_idea: Turn old cloth into cleaning rags, cushion covers or cloth bags.
eco_tip: Buy fewer, better-quality clothes and repair them when possible.
explanation: Fabric can be worn again, reused as rags or recycled, which keeps it out of landfill.

name: Sanitary pad / diaper
action: Wrap it in paper or a disposable bag, mark it as sanitary waste, and place it in the general (sanitary) waste bin. Never flush it.
reuse_idea: Reusable cloth pads or menstrual cups are options to reduce this waste.
eco_tip: Reusable hygiene products reduce waste over time.
explanation: Used hygiene products are not recyclable and need to be wrapped and kept separate for the safety of collectors.

name: Used face mask / gloves
action: Cut the straps, fold it, place it in a closed bag and put it in the general waste bin.
reuse_idea: Use washable cloth masks for everyday needs.
eco_tip: Straps can tangle animals, so cut them before throwing.
explanation: Disposable masks and gloves are made of mixed plastics and are not recyclable at home.

name: Cigarette butts
action: Make sure it is fully put out, then place it in the general waste bin. Do not litter.
reuse_idea: Not reusable.
eco_tip: Filters contain plastic fibres and chemicals, so quitting or using a portable ashtray helps.
explanation: Butts contain plastic filters and toxic residue, so they should go into the general waste.

name: Broken ceramic / crockery
action: Wrap sharp pieces in paper or cardboard, label them, and place them in the general waste.
reuse_idea: Use broken pieces as drainage at the bottom of plant pots or in mosaic crafts.
eco_tip: Donate chipped but safe items instead of throwing them.
explanation: Ceramics have a different melting point from glass, so they cannot go in glass recycling.

name: Paper cup / disposable cup
action: Empty it and place it in the general (reject) waste unless your area has a special cup-recycling programme. Do not mix it with clean paper.
reuse_idea: Reuse a clean cup once as a seedling pot.
eco_tip: Carry your own mug or ask for a reusable cup.
explanation: Paper cups usually have a thin plastic lining, so they cannot be recycled with ordinary paper.

name: Plastic straw / cutlery
action: Put it in the general (reject) waste unless a local facility says it accepts small plastic items.
reuse_idea: Not worth reusing. Choose a steel or bamboo alternative next time.
eco_tip: Say no to straws and disposable cutlery when you can.
explanation: Small, light plastic items are hard to sort at recycling plants and are rarely recycled.

name: Cotton / sponge / dust
action: Put it in the general (reject) waste bin.
reuse_idea: Hair and clean cotton can be added to compost in small amounts.
eco_tip: Choose natural, long-lasting cleaning tools like cloth over sponges.
explanation: Mixed household sweepings cannot be recycled or composted well, so they go to general waste.
